title: Your Soft Skills Baseline — School Edition
theme: Everyday decisions from school, friendships, sports, and online life
description: 10 real situations from school life to understand how you naturally think, decide, and connect with others. No right or wrong answers — just honest choices. Takes about 10 minutes.
learning_objectives: Understand your natural response style across 8 key soft skill dimensions
See how you handle pressure, fairness, and social situations
Identify where you're already strong and where you can grow
how_to_play: Read each situation carefully and pick the response that feels most like what you would actually do — not what you think a teacher would want to hear. Honest choices give you the most useful result.
psychological_framework: Situational judgment assessment based on behavioral decision theory

glossary_terms.definition: The process of choosing between different options after considering their consequences
Giving up one thing to gain another — every choice has a cost
A plan of action designed to achieve a long-term goal
The result or outcome of a choice or action
A particular way of looking at something — everyone has a different perspective

rounds.title: Group Project, Last Night
rounds.story: Your group project is due tomorrow. You've done your part. At 10 PM, your classmate Arjun messages you: 'I haven't started my section — there was a family emergency and I completely froze. I'm so sorry.' The rest of the group is asleep. If his section is missing, the whole submission will be incomplete.
rounds.goal: Decide how to respond to Arjun tonight
rounds.coaching_moment: How we respond when a teammate is struggling — especially under time pressure — says a lot about whether we lead with empathy or with self-interest.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever been in Arjun's position? What would you have wanted someone to do for you?

choices.label: Message him back, find out what he can still manage tonight, and offer to split the remaining work
choices.feedback: You checked in before assuming the worst and looked for a practical path forward together. That's the kind of response that builds real friendships — and real teams. It's not about absorbing all his work; it's about not leaving someone to fail alone when you can help.
choices.coaching_moment: The best teammates find out what's actually happening before deciding what to do. Empathy and strategy together are more powerful than either alone.

choices.label: Wake up the rest of the group in a group chat and let everyone decide together
choices.feedback: It feels fair to loop in everyone, but waking people at 10 PM and putting Arjun's emergency on display isn't really being fair to him. He trusted you first. Involving the group might be the right call eventually — but not before you've had a private conversation with him.
choices.coaching_moment: Transparency is important, but so is protecting someone's dignity. Always try a private conversation before a public one.

choices.label: Just do his section yourself quietly — the grade matters and arguing won't help at this point
choices.feedback: It's kind to want to fix things, but quietly covering for someone every time they fall short sets a pattern where they don't need to show up. It also burns you out. There's a difference between helping someone and doing everything for them — especially without a conversation.
choices.coaching_moment: Helping and over-functioning aren't the same thing. The most sustainable support comes with a conversation attached.

rounds.scene_hint: dimly lit bedroom, 10 PM, notification glow, group project stress

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: The Dare That Could Ruin Someone
rounds.story: Your friend group is on a WhatsApp chat. The 'popular' seniors are watching. Someone dares you to screenshot a classmate's embarrassing moment from a school event and post it with a mean caption. A few people are already laughing. One person says: 'Come on, do it — don't be boring.'
rounds.goal: Decide how you respond to the dare
rounds.coaching_moment: The moments that test who you are the most are always the ones where the people around you are watching and waiting.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Think of a time you felt pressured to do something that didn't feel right. What made it hard to say no?

choices.label: Say no clearly — 'That's not something I'm going to do' — and leave it at that
choices.feedback: This takes more courage than it looks. Saying no without a long explanation — just a calm, clear 'I'm not doing that' — is actually one of the strongest social moves you can make. People respect boundaries stated without apology, even if they don't say so in the moment.
choices.coaching_moment: You don't need to justify a 'no.' A clear boundary stated once, calmly, is stronger than a long explanation.

choices.label: Do it — it's just a joke and you don't want to be the one who kills the mood
choices.feedback: It might feel like just a joke, but the person in that screenshot will experience it very differently. 'Not wanting to kill the mood' is a real feeling — but it's worth noticing that their comfort mattered more to you than a classmate's dignity. That's worth sitting with.
choices.coaching_moment: Fitting in by hurting someone else is a trade-off. The question is whether you'd want to make it if you were the person being posted about.

choices.label: Change the topic or make a joke to redirect the group's attention without directly refusing
choices.feedback: Redirecting the energy takes quick thinking and it can work — it protects the classmate while keeping the social temperature down. The one thing to watch: if the redirect fails and they come back to the dare, you'll eventually need a clear answer. Deflection only buys time.
choices.coaching_moment: Creative redirection is a real social skill — but it works best as a first move, not a permanent substitute for a clear boundary.

rounds.image_prompt: teenager looking at phone in a group setting, peer pressure visible, conflicted expression
rounds.scene_hint: school common area, group dynamics, social pressure moment

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: The Answer Sheet
rounds.story: You're in the middle of a Class 10 board exam. One question is worth 8 marks and you're completely stuck — your mind has gone blank. The student next to you, Priya, quietly slides her answer sheet slightly toward you. It's clearly visible. The invigilator has their back turned.
rounds.goal: Decide what you do in this moment
rounds.coaching_moment: The choices we make when no one is watching — especially when something is at stake — define our actual values, not just the ones we say we have.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever been tempted to take a shortcut that no one would have caught? What made you do it or not do it?

choices.label: Look away and write whatever you can on your own, even if it means losing those marks
choices.feedback: This is genuinely hard when 8 marks could change your result. But you chose your own integrity over a borrowed answer — that's not small. The score you earn honestly tells you something real about where you stand. A copied score doesn't.
choices.coaching_moment: A grade earned with someone else's answer doesn't belong to you. Only the grades you earn honestly measure your actual progress.

choices.label: Quickly copy what you need — Priya offered, the invigilator isn't watching, and it's a small risk
choices.feedback: Priya offering doesn't make it okay — and 'a small risk' isn't really about the risk of getting caught. It's about what you're willing to let yourself get away with. Each time it becomes a little easier. Board exams are designed to measure you — copying returns a false reading.
choices.coaching_moment: Every time we take a shortcut we don't need to, we make it slightly easier to take the next one. That's the real cost.

choices.label: Gently signal to Priya to move her sheet away — protect both of you from getting caught
choices.feedback: You looked out for Priya as much as yourself — that's thoughtful. By signalling her away, you protected her from an unnecessary risk she may not have fully considered. This shows both integrity and care for someone else's wellbeing.
choices.coaching_moment: Real integrity isn't just about protecting yourself — sometimes it means protecting others from their own risky impulses.

rounds.scene_hint: exam hall, board exam tension, ethical crossroads

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: The New Kid Who's Stealing Your Spot
rounds.story: You've been on the school basketball team for two years. A new student, Rahul, joined this term. He's enthusiastic but still learning. Your coach has been giving Rahul more practice time and playing him in positions you used to fill — even in the last two matches where the team lost. Your teammates are frustrated too.
rounds.goal: Decide how you respond to this situation
rounds.coaching_moment: When we feel overlooked despite working hard, how we handle that says a lot about our emotional maturity and our ability to think beyond our own situation.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Think of a time someone got something you felt you deserved more. What was your first reaction? What do you wish it had been?

choices.label: Ask the coach for a one-on-one conversation to understand what you need to do to earn back more playing time
choices.feedback: Going directly to the coach — not to complain, but to ask what you need to improve — is exactly the right move. It shows maturity, self-awareness, and the ability to channel frustration into something useful. Most coaches respond very well to this kind of conversation.
choices.coaching_moment: The strongest response to feeling overlooked isn't resentment — it's asking the question that actually helps you move forward.

choices.label: Vent to the team about how unfair the coach's decisions are and see if they'll back you up
choices.feedback: Your frustration is real and valid. But rallying teammates against the coach creates an environment where everyone is competing instead of playing together. It also puts your teammates in an uncomfortable position and rarely changes the coach's decisions. You end up with more resentment and less playing time.
choices.coaching_moment: Venting feels good in the short term but builds problems in the long term. The energy spent on blame rarely improves your actual situation.

choices.label: Accept it quietly and keep training hard — if you keep showing up, the coach will notice
choices.feedback: Staying focused and working hard without making it a drama shows maturity and resilience. The one risk is that staying silent sometimes means the coach doesn't know you're still hungry for more playing time. There's a version of this that combines patience with one honest conversation.
choices.coaching_moment: Patience and persistence are genuinely valuable — but speaking up for yourself when it matters isn't the same as complaining.

rounds.image_prompt: teen athlete watching from bench as a new player gets coaching attention, processing complex emotions
rounds.scene_hint: school basketball court, unfair feeling, competitive and emotional

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: What Do You Do With Your Best Friend's Secret?
rounds.story: Your best friend Sneha confided in you two weeks ago that she's been skipping school and forging attendance notes. She begged you not to tell anyone. Today, your class teacher stopped you in the corridor and said: 'I've been noticing Sneha's absences. Do you know what's going on with her? Is she okay?'
rounds.goal: Decide what you say to the teacher
rounds.coaching_moment: When loyalty to a friend and concern for their wellbeing point in different directions, there's no clean answer — but how you think through it reveals a lot about your values.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Has a friend ever trusted you with something difficult? What made it hard to decide what to do with that trust?

choices.label: Tell the teacher honestly what you know — you're worried Sneha might actually need help
choices.feedback: This is hard, and Sneha might be upset. But if she's been skipping school regularly, something may be going on that's bigger than just bunking. Telling a trusted adult because you're genuinely worried for her is different from betraying her — it's protecting her. Real friendship sometimes means doing the uncomfortable thing.
choices.coaching_moment: There's a difference between keeping a secret that's harmless and keeping one that might be covering up someone's struggle. Choosing their wellbeing over their comfort is sometimes the braver kind of loyalty.

choices.label: Say you're not sure and deflect — you don't want to break Sneha's trust
choices.feedback: Protecting a friend's secret is important to you, and that's understandable. But 'not sure' when you clearly know something puts you in a tricky position if the teacher probes further — and it doesn't help Sneha if something is actually wrong. At minimum, this should push you to talk to Sneha directly before the situation escalates.
choices.coaching_moment: Deflecting doesn't make a problem go away — it just delays the moment you'll need to deal with it, usually when it's bigger.

choices.label: Don't say anything now, but go to Sneha immediately after and tell her the teacher is asking questions
choices.feedback: Alerting Sneha gives her the chance to address things herself before they spiral. You're respecting her agency and giving her the information she needs to make a choice. This works best if you also have an honest conversation with her about whether she's actually okay — not just covering her tracks.
choices.coaching_moment: Giving someone information they need to handle their own situation can be a form of care — as long as you're not enabling something that's harming them.

rounds.scene_hint: school corridor, trust dilemma, caring but torn expression

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Boards in 3 Weeks. But the Game Just Dropped.
rounds.story: Your board exams — the ones that determine which stream you get in Class 11 — are exactly 3 weeks away. A new game your whole friend group has been excited about just launched. Everyone's playing every evening. Your evenings are usually when you do your best studying. The group chat is already going non-stop.
rounds.goal: Choose how you handle the next 3 weeks
rounds.coaching_moment: The ability to delay short-term fun for long-term goals — especially when everyone around you is doing the opposite — is one of the most reliable predictors of long-term success.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Think of a time you chose short-term fun over something important. How did it feel afterwards? What would you do differently?

choices.label: Mute the group chat and tell your friends you're going offline until after exams — boards come first
choices.feedback: This takes real discipline, especially when FOMO is pulling hard. You're not saying gaming is bad — you're saying this three-week window matters too much to compromise. The game will still be there after exams. Class 11 stream choices are much harder to undo.
choices.coaching_moment: The difference between people who reach their goals and people who don't often isn't talent — it's the ability to protect their time for a few critical weeks.

choices.label: Join your friends — you'll feel left out if you don't, and you can still study in the mornings
choices.feedback: FOMO is real and it matters. But 'I'll study in the mornings' is a plan that sounds reasonable and rarely survives contact with late-night gaming. If your best study time is evenings, this trade-off has a real cost. The fun is real; so is what you're giving up.
choices.coaching_moment: Most people underestimate how much small daily choices compound over three weeks. Every evening you trade for gaming, you're borrowing against exam day.

choices.label: Set a rule: 1 hour of gaming as a reward after hitting your daily study target
choices.feedback: Using gaming as a reward after studying is a genuinely good strategy — it gives you something to work toward and protects your study time. The key is whether you actually stick to the target before starting. If the rule is enforced, this is smart. If gaming happens regardless of targets, the rule is just a story you're telling yourself.
choices.coaching_moment: Reward-based systems work when the reward actually requires the work. The quality of the rule depends entirely on whether you keep it.

expert_pick.reason: Research shows that patience-based decisions lead to 3x better long-term outcomes.

rounds.title: Going Viral for the Wrong Reason
rounds.story: You posted a thoughtful comment on a school event Instagram page — something you genuinely cared about. A student from another school with 8,000 followers screenshot it, posted it with a mocking caption, and tagged their followers. The comments are rolling in. Some are mean. Your own friends have seen it. Your stomach is in knots.
rounds.goal: Decide how you respond to this
rounds.coaching_moment: How you bounce back from public embarrassment — without losing yourself or retaliating in ways you'll regret — is a form of resilience that will serve you long after school ends.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Have you ever been publicly embarrassed? What did you do first? What do you wish you had done?

choices.label: Ignore the post entirely — responding will only give it more attention and extend the cycle
choices.feedback: This is often the smartest play. Online pile-ons run on engagement — any response, including a defensive one, adds fuel. Going quiet is not the same as being weak. It's understanding how attention works and denying it the thing it needs to spread.
choices.coaching_moment: The most powerful response to trolling is often no response at all. Your silence doesn't mean you lost — it means you chose not to play.

choices.label: Post a sharp, witty reply that shows you're unbothered and lets people see you handle it with confidence
choices.feedback: A genuinely good reply can reframe the narrative and earn you respect. The risk is that a sharp reply can escalate if it lands wrong or invites more responses from their followers. This works best if you're genuinely unbothered — it falls flat if the reply shows any hurt beneath the words.
choices.coaching_moment: Wit works when it comes from calm confidence. If you reply while upset, it usually reads as upset — no matter how clever the words are.

choices.label: Screenshot the post, send it to their school, and report the account for cyberbullying
choices.feedback: Reporting targeted mockery is entirely appropriate and not an overreaction. You have a right to protect yourself from harassment, and formal reporting creates a record. Just make sure you're doing it because you want to protect yourself — not purely for retaliation. Those are different motivations with different outcomes.
choices.coaching_moment: Reporting harassment is not weak — it's using the right tools for the right problem. Just make sure you're doing it to protect yourself, not to hurt them.

rounds.image_prompt: teenager looking distressed at phone, screenshot going viral, supportive friend in background
rounds.scene_hint: school environment, online mockery, resilience moment

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: The Grade That Doesn't Add Up
rounds.story: You worked genuinely hard on your Hindi project — three weeks, original research, a presentation with charts you made yourself. You got 32/50. Your friend Manu, who you know pasted content from Wikipedia and put in maybe two hours, got 43/50. Your teacher announced grades publicly. You feel angry and confused.
rounds.goal: Decide how you respond to this grade
rounds.coaching_moment: Unfair outcomes are a part of life. What separates people who grow from them is not whether they feel the anger — it's what they do with it.
rounds.reflection_prompt: When did you last feel an outcome was deeply unfair? What did you do? What do you wish you had done instead?

choices.label: Request a private meeting with the teacher to understand the marking criteria and ask for feedback on your specific work
choices.feedback: This is mature and strategic. You're not attacking the teacher — you're trying to understand the gap between your effort and your result. Teachers almost always respond better to this kind of direct, respectful inquiry than to complaints. The feedback, even if it stings, will make your next submission better.
choices.coaching_moment: Asking 'how do I understand this result?' is always more useful than 'this is unfair.' The first gets you information; the second just expresses the feeling.

choices.label: Tell your parents and ask them to speak to the teacher on your behalf
choices.feedback: Having parents intervene isn't always wrong — there are times an adult advocate is needed. But doing it as your first move, without trying to resolve it yourself, misses an important chance to practice standing up for yourself. Most teachers will also be more open to a student's question than to a parent's complaint.
choices.coaching_moment: Building the ability to advocate for yourself — calmly and directly — is one of the most important things you can learn in school. It serves you long after grades stop mattering.

choices.label: Accept it and move on — teachers have reasons you don't see, and fighting grades creates more trouble than it's worth
choices.feedback: Accepting unfairness without drama shows composure, and sometimes that's the right call. But there's a version of 'accepting it' that's actually avoidance — you stay quiet because confrontation feels scary, not because you've genuinely processed it. The middle path is asking a respectful question, not demanding a new grade.
choices.coaching_moment: Acceptance and resignation are different things. Accepting an outcome after seeking clarity is healthy. Staying quiet because you're afraid to ask is a different thing.

achievements.title: Baseline Established
achievements.description: Completed your School Edition Soft Skills Baseline

transfer_exercises: This week, notice one moment where you felt peer pressure to do something that didn't feel right. Write down what you did and what you wish you'd done.
Think of one person in your class who you haven't been kind to recently. Find a small way to show you see them this week.
Next time you have a big exam or deadline coming, notice what you choose to do the evening before. Is it the choice you'd recommend to a friend?
coaching_moment: Setbacks are not failures — they are lessons. Bouncing back stronger is what truly matters.

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.
